common_name: Little Lemon Twist Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Small Crispate Yellow)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Patricia R. Cochenour in 2008, Little Lemon Twist is a small-flowered, unusual-form crispate diploid daylily with clear lemon-yellow self blooms about 3.25 inches across, their pinched and twisted segments carried well above the foliage on 32-inch scapes. Dormant and blooming in midseason, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 2017. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Baby Blue Eyes Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Lavender Watermark Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Hybridized by Elizabeth Shooter and registered in 1998, Baby Blue Eyes is a small-flowered, semi-evergreen diploid daylily with light lavender-purple blooms about four inches across, marked with purple veins and a washed blue watermark eyezone above a chartreuse throat, carried on 20-inch scapes with roughly 17 buds on three branches. It blooms and reblooms through midseason and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 2011. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Her Best Bloomers Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Fuchsia Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Dr. Donald M. Herr in 2001, Her Best Bloomers is a heavy-budded, dormant diploid daylily bearing small fuchsia-red flowers about four inches across with a darker red eye above a yellow-green throat, on 28-inch scapes carrying around 30 buds across five branches. It blooms in midseason and went on to win the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 2007. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Spacecoast Sweetness Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Pink Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Hybridized by John L. Kinnebrew Jr. and registered in 1998, Spacecoast Sweetness is a small-flowered, semi-evergreen tetraploid daylily with a clear pink self bloom roughly four inches across on 21-inch scapes. It opens in the early season with dependable rebloom and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 2004; it later contributed as a parent of the registered cultivar 'Spacecoast Sweet Eye'. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Tigerling Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Orange with Red Eyezone)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Patrick Stamile in 1989, Tigerling is a fragrant, dormant tetraploid daylily with small, ruffled light-orange flowers about 3.75 inches across, marked with a bright red eyezone above a green throat, on 25-inch scapes. It blooms and reblooms through midseason and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 1998. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Exotic Echo Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Pink-Cream with Burgundy Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Sellers in 1984, Exotic Echo is a compact, small-flowered daylily bearing a pink-cream blend bloom about three inches across with a double burgundy eyezone above a green throat, on scapes around 16 inches tall. It opens in midseason and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 1993. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Wynnson Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Bright Yellow Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Olin W. Criswell in 1977, Wynnson is a dormant diploid daylily with small, bright yellow self flowers about 4.5 inches across on 24-inch scapes, unscented but long-lasting with an extended, diurnal bloom habit. Opening in the early-midseason, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling in 1984. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Little Infant Daylily (Annie T. Giles Award, Small-Flowered Parent Line)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Hybridized by Monette and registered in 1977, Little Infant is a small-flowered daylily that won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered seedling that same year. It went on to influence later small-flowered breeding lines, appearing in the parentage of registered cultivars such as 'Alyne Fisher' and 'Inez Tarrant'. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Walter Kennedy Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Red with Darker Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Patrick Stamile in 2008, Walter Kennedy is a high-bud-count, evergreen tetraploid daylily with red flowers nearly six inches across, deepened by a darker red eye and matching edge above a green throat, on 28-inch scapes showing eight-way branching and 46 or more buds. An early-morning opener that reblooms through midseason, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 2019, after earning an AHS Honorable Mention in 2013 and Award of Merit in 2016. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: God Save the Queen Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Orchid with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Morss in 2005, God Save the Queen is an evergreen tetraploid daylily with large, 7-inch medium orchid blooms showing a midnight-purple eye and a purple-outlined, yellow-gold filigree edge above a yellow-green throat, on 30-inch scapes carrying about 26 buds across four branches. Blooming in the early season with reliable rebloom, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 2018. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Marked by Lydia Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Yellow Spider with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Temple in 1994, Marked by Lydia is a semi-evergreen diploid spider daylily with narrow-petaled, medium-yellow flowers about 8.5 inches across, marked with a purple eyezone above a green throat, on 29-inch scapes. An early bloomer with an extended flowering period and rebloom, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award in 2000 and the Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 2005, having already received an AHS Honorable Mention in 1999 and Award of Merit in 2003. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Brookwood Lee Causey Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Golden Yellow with Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Hybridized by Leo Sharp and registered in 1998, Brookwood Lee Causey is a fragrant, semi-evergreen diploid daylily with recurved, golden-yellow flowers about 4.75 inches across, marked with a bright red eye above a green throat, on compact 18-inch scapes showing three-way branching and about 14 buds. It blooms in midseason and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 2003, after an AHS Honorable Mention in 2002 and ahead of an Award of Merit in 2005. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Canadian Border Patrol Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Cream with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by E.H. Salter in 1995, Canadian Border Patrol is a semi-evergreen tetraploid daylily with pale ivory-cream flowers about six inches across, marked by a large deep-purple eyezone and a dark, ruffled picotee edge above a lime-green throat, on 28-inch scapes. Opening in the early-midseason with reliable rebloom, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 2000. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Pirate's Patch Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Ivory Cream with Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by E.H. Salter in 1991 from a cross of Well of Souls and Jungle Mask, Pirate's Patch is an evergreen tetraploid daylily with ivory-cream flowers about six inches across, marked by a dark, rich purple eyezone and a thin matching picotee above a yellow-green throat, on 28-inch scapes. Opening in the early-midseason with rebloom, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 1997, following an AHS Honorable Mention in 1995. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Bette Davis Eyes Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award, Lavender with Grape-Purple Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by David Kirchhoff in 1982, Bette Davis Eyes is a fragrant, evergreen diploid daylily with lavender flowers about 5.25 inches across, deepened by a grape-purple eye, on 23-inch scapes. Opening in the early season, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or patterned cultivar in 1986, after a Junior Citation in 1982 and ahead of an AHS Honorable Mention in 1987 and Award of Merit in 1991. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Pumpkin Britches Daylily (Lambert/Webster Award, Unusual Form Cascade)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Eric Simpson in 2016 from a cross of Birds of a Feather and Dances with Giraffes, Pumpkin Britches is a dormant diploid daylily with large, veined orange-bitone flowers about 8.5 inches across, showing a darker orange band above a yellow-green throat and curling, twisting unusual-form cascade segments, on 40-inch scapes carrying about 18 buds across three branches. Blooming in midseason, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lambert/Webster Award for best unusual-form daylily in 2022. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Dances with Giraffes Daylily (Lambert/Webster Award, Unusual Form Cascade)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Margo Reed in 2005, Dances with Giraffes is a very tall unusual-form cascade daylily with golden-yellow flowers about eight inches across, blushed with a rose-peach eye above a green throat, their long petals and tightly corkscrewed sepals cascading from scapes that commonly reach five feet. Blooming midseason to late with 26 to 30 buds on two branches, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lambert/Webster Award for best unusual-form daylily in 2019, after an AHS Honorable Mention in 2009 and Award of Merit in 2014. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering, and stake tall scapes in exposed, windy sites.

common_name: Christmas in Oz Daylily (Lambert/Webster Award, Pink with Red Chevron Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Katisue Herrington in 2004, Christmas in Oz is a semi-evergreen diploid daylily with huge, crispate-cascade unusual-form blooms about nine inches across in bright pink, marked with a vivid red chevron eyezone over a light grass-green throat that fades to citron yellow, veined with white midribs, on 36-inch scapes showing five-way branching and about 36 buds. It blooms and reblooms through midseason and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lambert/Webster Award for best unusual-form daylily in 2013. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Frilly Bliss Daylily (Lambert/Webster Award, Powder Pink Cascade)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Jan Joiner in 1998, Frilly Bliss is an evergreen diploid daylily with large, nine-inch unusual-form cascade blooms in powder pink, washed with a rose halo, on 34-inch scapes. It opens in the mid-to-late season and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lambert/Webster Award for best unusual-form daylily in 2005. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: All American Windmill Daylily (Lambert/Webster Award, Unusual Form Crispate)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Clarence J. Crochet in 1995 from a cross of Copper Windmill and Yellow Angel, All American Windmill is a dormant diploid daylily with light-orange polychrome flowers about seven inches across, deepened by a dark orange eye, their curling and pinched crispate segments carried on 26-inch scapes. Blooming in the early-midseason with rebloom, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lambert/Webster Award for best unusual-form daylily in 2004, after an AHS Honorable Mention in 1999. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: WYSIWYG Daylily (Ida Munson Award, Rose-Pink Peach Bitone Double)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Scott Elliott in 2013, WYSIWYG is a very fragrant, semi-evergreen diploid daylily that is double about 99 percent of the time, with rose-pink and pale-peach bitone flowers around 6.5 inches across, streaked with cream, dark rose, and dark peach above a green throat, its crispate-cascade segments carried on scapes with roughly 18 buds across three branches. Blooming mid-to-late season with rebloom, it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award for best double-flowered daylily in 2017, after an Honorable Mention in 2016 and ahead of an Award of Merit in 2019. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Wildman George Daylily (Ida Munson Award, Orange Bitone Double)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Scott Elliott in 2010, Wildman George is a very fragrant, evergreen diploid daylily that is double about 95 percent of the time, with orange-bitone flowers about six inches across, deepened by a dark red-orange halo above a yellow-green throat and crispate segments, on 34-inch scapes carrying roughly 28 buds across four branches. It blooms early with dependable rebloom and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award for best double-flowered daylily in 2015. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Jelly Filled Donut Daylily (Ida Munson Award, Yellow with Red Eye Double)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Nancy Eller in 2004, Jelly Filled Donut is a slightly fragrant, semi-evergreen tetraploid daylily with large double flowers more than 4.5 inches across in bright yellow, marked with a red eye above a green throat. It blooms and reblooms early in the season and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award for best double-flowered daylily in 2014. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Amanda's Little Red Shoes Daylily (Ida Munson Award, Rose Red with White Edge Double)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun; divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

directions: Registered by Nancy Eller in 2004 from a cross of Stellar Double Rose and Reba My Love, Amanda's Little Red Shoes is a fragrant, semi-evergreen diploid daylily that is double about 98 percent of the time, with rose-red flowers about six inches across edged in white above a yellow throat, on 24-inch scapes carrying about 20 buds across three branches. It blooms early with rebloom and won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award for best double-flowered daylily in 2013. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.
